title: Housing supply is expanding unevenly while affordability, mobility, household formation, and immigration reshape who can access place
source_unit: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, The State of the Nation’s Housing 2026
geography: United States; national housing, household-formation, mobility, affordability, demographic, and regional analysis

observations.period: 2025-2026; housing construction, vacancies, and low-cost supply

denominator.unit: U.S. housing market and new construction pipeline

new_multifamily_asking_rent.unit: dollars median asking rent for new multifamily units in 2025

new_single_family_price.unit: dollars approximate median price of a new single-family home in 2025

affordable_listings_under_75000_income.unit: percent of listings affordable to households earning $75,000 or less in March 2026

affordable_listings_2019.unit: percent of listings affordable to households earning $75,000 or less in March 2019

mechanism.value: More construction or vacancy does not automatically create reachable low-cost housing when land, materials, financing, and market incentives concentrate new supply at higher prices

observations.method: Harvard JCHS synthesis of Census, housing-market, construction, vacancy, listing, and affordability data.
observations.uncertainty: Listing affordability is a market snapshot and does not measure actual transaction access, subsidies, credit approval, neighborhood quality, or all housing costs.
observations.subgroup: Households earning $75,000 or less, lower-income renters, first-time buyers, and households in markets with high land and construction costs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher-cost new construction can free older units over time, and vacancy increases may eventually moderate rents even if immediate access remains unequal.

denominator.unit: U.S. households measured in the American Community Survey

annual_mobility.unit: percent of households relocating in the prior 12 months in 2024

mobility_trend.value: The 2024 mobility share was the lowest point in the 20-year ACS history, driven by declining homeowner mobility while renter mobility remained roughly stable

mechanism.value: Housing costs and mortgage-rate lock-in can reduce the ability to move toward jobs, care, schools, safety, or better-fitting housing, turning place into constraint

observations.method: JCHS analysis of ACS household mobility and related mortgage-rate and housing-market data.
observations.uncertainty: Low mobility does not distinguish voluntary stability from constrained immobility; the report does not estimate the causal contribution of mortgage lock-in versus jobs, family, health, or local preferences.
observations.subgroup: Homeowners with below-market mortgage rates, younger households, renters with different lease options, and households needing to move for work or care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Staying can indicate neighborhood attachment, improved housing stability, or satisfaction rather than an inability to move.

observations.period: 2024-2026; migration, household formation, and regional population change

states_prevented_population_loss.unit: states where immigration prevented aggregate population loss between 2021 and 2025

mechanism.value: Migration policy changes affect housing demand, rental formation, population growth, labor supply, and the fiscal-demographic base of places

observations.method: JCHS synthesis of Census Population Estimates Program, ACS household formation, and housing-market data.
observations.uncertainty: The projection is not a realized future count; migration estimates do not establish the cause of housing costs or the distribution of benefits and pressures across local markets.
observations.subgroup: Recent immigrants, renter households, states dependent on immigration for population growth, and communities experiencing changing demand for housing and services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower immigration can reduce rental demand in some markets while weakening labor supply, population growth, and housing construction capacity in others.

denominator.unit: U.S. homebuyers, homeowners, and renter households in JCHS affordability analysis

first_time_buyer_share.unit: percent of homebuyers between mid-2024 and mid-2025 who were first-time buyers

median_first_time_buyer_age.unit: years median age of first-time homebuyers

severely_cost_burdened_homeowners.unit: million homeowner households spending more than half of income on housing and utilities in 2024

renter_cost_burden.unit: percent of renter households cost burdened in 2024 according to JCHS figure summary

mechanism.value: Housing cost burden delays household formation and first purchase while compressing money available for food, care, mobility, health, and civic or cultural participation

observations.method: JCHS analysis of Census ACS, Housing Vacancy Survey, and homebuyer data using moderate and severe cost-burden thresholds.
observations.uncertainty: Cost burden is a ratio measure and does not capture household composition, wealth, housing quality, informal support, or the full range of nonhousing expenses.
observations.subgroup: First-time buyers, families with children, cost-burdened renters and homeowners, and households with limited residual income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some households choose higher housing costs for quality, location, or services; cost burden does not by itself prove deprivation or delayed family formation.

related_sources.claim: Harvard JCHS report landing page and related housing data resources.
Census ACS source underlying mobility, cost-burden, and demographic tabulations.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. structural housing route from construction and market supply through low-cost availability, residential mobility, immigration, household formation, first-time buying, and cost burden. It is a secondary synthesis of public housing and demographic data, not a household panel, causal land-use evaluation, or proof that any single policy caused mobility or affordability changes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Harvard JCHS 2026 report PDF was reviewed for construction and low-cost supply, affordability, mobility, migration and household formation, first-time buying, and cost-burden findings.
